paragraphs: The following judgments concern the everyday service practices of manicurists and pedicurists. They do not predict hiring, licensing, qualification, or income outcomes.

The core work of manicurists and pedicurists is to clean and shape clients' fingernails and toenails under hygienic conditions: clean and disinfect tools and the work area, use water and oil to soften cuticles, trim and file nails, apply base coat and color or decorations, and add extensions or reinforcing wraps when needed. They also assess hands and nail surfaces, advise on care and products, maintain supply inventories and service records, schedule appointments, and collect payments.

Entirely fictional task package: provide a fictional client service form and equipment list, including 1 appointment and requirements record, 1 equipment and disinfection checklist, and 1 scenario for observing nail conditions and contraindications. Within 60 minutes, write service steps, cleaning and disinfection procedures, matters to confirm with the client, circumstances requiring a pause and escalation, and records to retain. Do not use real client information.

Sample output and reflection: check whether needs and contraindications were confirmed first, cleaning and disinfection preceded service steps, safe use of equipment and chemicals was explained, and records and escalation routes were clear. Then ask yourself whether you can stand for long periods and repeat fine hand movements, maintain hygiene standards during peak appointments, and willingly explain care and products to clients.

On this page, manicurists and pedicurists refers to O*NET 39-5092.00: workers who clean and shape clients' fingernails and toenails and may polish or decorate them, including job titles such as manicurist, nail technician, and pedicurist. Work includes cleaning and disinfecting tools and the environment, treating cuticles, trimming and filing nails, applying base coat and color, adding extensions or reinforcing wraps, assessing hands and nail surfaces, advising on care and products, maintaining inventory and service records, scheduling appointments, and collecting payments. Work mainly takes place indoors in nail salons, salons, or client service settings. This page excludes adjacent occupations such as barbers; hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists; skincare specialists; and shampooers.

entries: Inputs: clients' fingernails and toenails and their condition, appointment and requirements information, nail tools and disposable supplies, disinfectants and chemicals such as nail polish, solvents, powders, and polish remover, products and color charts, service and inventory records, and payment and appointment systems.

Checkable outputs: cleaned and shaped nails with completed color or decoration, disinfected tools and workstations, assessments and care advice for nail and hand conditions, service and inventory records, appointment and payment records, and explanations when referral or escalation is needed.

Complete workflow: check the appointment and requirements → inspect hands and nail surfaces and confirm contraindications → clean and disinfect tools and the workstation → treat cuticles and trim and file nails → apply base coat and color or decorations, with extensions or reinforcement when needed → inspect the result and confirm it with the client → record the service and inventory and collect payment.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether a client's hand or nail condition makes service unsuitable and requires referral, whether tools and workstations meet cleaning and disinfection requirements, whether chemical use and ventilation are safe, whether nail shape and decoration meet the client's needs, and whether to pause and escalate when abnormalities arise.

Environment and pace: service is usually performed seated for long periods in a nail salon or salon, potentially leaning forward and repeating fine hand movements, with exposure to product vapors and dust. Full-time work is common, alongside part-time, evening, and weekend schedules. Check actual demands against the workstation, ventilation, and appointment procedures.

Research inputs: occupational identity, tasks, work activities, work context, skills and knowledge, interest code, education, and Job Zone for O*NET 39-5092.00. Wage, employment, and industry data on that page cover this occupation. Research conclusions do not establish qualifications, licensing, wages, or employment measures for mainland China.

Check first: the official occupational scope, actual employer requirements, education or training, local licensing and hygiene rules, supervised tasks, and safety boundaries for tools, chemicals, and clients.

End-to-end work: start by checking the appointment and requirements, then inspect nail conditions, clean and disinfect, trim and file, apply color and decoration, inspect the result, record the service, and collect payment. Do not start service until all hygiene and safety conditions are met, or continue until any nail or skin abnormality has been clarified.

Boundaries with adjacent roles: this page covers only manicurists and pedicurists. Barbers cut hair and shave; hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists cut and color hair and provide facial care; skincare specialists provide facial skincare; shampooers wash hair and care for the scalp. Their service subjects and authorizations are not interchangeable with this occupation.

Barbers mainly provide haircuts, facial grooming, and shaving. Manicurists and pedicurists focus on cleaning, shaping, coloring, and decorating fingernails and toenails, using different tools on different service subjects.

Hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists provide haircuts, coloring, perms, and facial care. Manicurists and pedicurists focus on nail care and decoration. They may work in the same salon, but their authorizations and qualifications must be checked separately.

Skincare specialists focus on analyzing and caring for facial skin; manicurists and pedicurists focus on nails and hands. Both should refer skin or nail abnormalities rather than treat them themselves.
Shampooers wash hair and care for the scalp; manicurists and pedicurists care for nails and hands. Their work focus and required licenses differ.
Boundaries of AI's impact on manicurists and pedicurists

Editorial task hypothesis: validated tools may assist with appointments, inventory records, or style references, while generative AI may draft communications using fictional material. Ordinary scheduling software is not equivalent to generative AI. This page has not obtained studies of AI adoption or job outcomes in nail services; product and health advice still requires human verification. AI Impact Score 33% is an editorial estimate. Occupational sources describe the actual tasks and subjects involved: nails and hands, tools and disinfection, chemicals and products, appointments and records. Tool capabilities, organizational adoption, and job outcomes are recorded separately; wage or employment data is not used as AI evidence.

Editorial comparison: organizing information and drafting may receive assistance, but actual adoption depends on systems, data authorization, and review conditions. This does not permit omitting hands-on nail treatment or disinfection, or the associated responsibility.

Human control points: confirm client needs and contraindications, assess nail and skin conditions, carry out cleaning and disinfection, use chemicals safely, take responsibility for the finished work and client safety, and comply with local licensing and hygiene rules.

First conduct an offline exercise using entirely fictional appointment and requirements records. Write service steps, disinfection procedures, chemical safety measures, and escalation boundaries without relying on unverified automated advice to replace on-site judgment.
Editorial hypothesis: first test tool outputs using fictional appointment records. A software skills list does not demonstrate generative AI adoption or effectiveness.
Check product instructions, client information, and the service scope. Do not treat automated suggestions as a basis for diagnosis or infection management; human on-site judgment is still required.

This does not establish that no domestic sources publish occupational data.

US wage and employment scope for manicurists and pedicurists, occupation 39-5092.00

In 2025, the US nationwide median wage for this occupation was 35,760 dollars annually and 17.19 dollars hourly; P10 and P90 annual wages were 28,920 and 50,140 dollars, respectively. Older employment facts retain the 2024—2034 version; 24,800 is projected average annual openings, not a ten-year total. The latest BLS figures are 201,800 jobs in 2025, 9% growth in 2025—2035, and 21,900 average annual openings. Treat these versions separately.

Wage statistical reference: 2025 BLS OEWS, US nationwide occupation 39-5092.00. Annual and hourly wages are listed separately as in the original table. They do not represent an individual's annual hours, take-home income, or beginner level.

P10/25/50/75/90 denotes positions in the wage distribution, not seniority levels. Annual and hourly wage percentiles do not convert an individual's working hours. Interpret employment counts, projected average annual openings, and individual hiring chances separately.

Industry reference within the occupation: the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook reports a median hourly wage of 17.19 dollars in personal care services for May 2025. Exact wages for other industries were not obtained and are not filled using the overall median. Industry shares of employers are also not wages or demand growth.

Employment scope: the 2024—2034 facts retained on this page and the latest 2025—2035 projections are different versions. Both the older 24,800 and newer 21,900 figures are average annual job openings, including replacements for workers who change occupations or leave, not net new jobs or ten-year totals.
Fit signals: start with observable work behavior

To assess fit, first observe hygiene procedures, fine hand movements, communication about needs, and escalation of abnormalities. Check actual demands from prolonged sitting, repeated forward-leaning movements, and chemical exposure. Interest tools and paper exercises cannot establish physical tolerance, operational competence, or qualifications.

Positive signals: willingness to follow hygiene procedures, fine and steady hand movements, patience and attention to detail, willingness to communicate with clients, and the ability to recognize abnormalities and proactively escalate them.

Reasons for caution: if prolonged sitting or repeated fine movements cause discomfort, product contact or odors cause discomfort, or disinfection and pause procedures are difficult to maintain, first check the workstation and safety controls and seek an appropriate professional assessment. Do not explain health demands through personality labels.

Trial activity: using entirely fictional appointment and requirements records, rehearse service steps, disinfection procedures, and escalation boundaries, and ask someone else to review them against the records.

The O*NET interest code is RC (Realistic–Conventional), emphasizing hands-on work and organizing information according to procedures. These labels describe activity preferences only and cannot determine competence or qualifications.

General personality measures such as the Big Five do not provide evidence about this occupation's job requirements and can only support self-reflection. Continue checking through actual experiences of manicure and pedicure work, client communication, and hygiene implementation.
Type-based tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications and can only support self-reflection.

Entry pathways and capability stages

O*NET Job Zone 1–2 describes preparation for an occupational group, not a uniform education requirement or training duration for nail technicians. BLS states that this occupation typically requires a state-approved cosmetology or nail program and a state examination for licensing. Check age, high-school education, and other specific requirements with the state authority.

United States: check state-approved programs, examinations, licensing, and reciprocity requirements. O*NET lists Manicurist as a registered apprenticeship occupation, but this does not prove a local program is available or that licensing is unnecessary. Mainland China: this research did not establish an exact occupational qualification mapping. Check actual services, local business hygiene requirements, and personnel requirements separately; do not assert that qualifications do not exist.

Education, training, certification, and licensing are different statuses. Completing training or obtaining industry certification does not automatically grant a license to practice. Check requirements for independently serving clients and collecting payment by state and locality; hygiene and safety conclusions must follow the competent authority's rules.

Entry stage: practice tool preparation and disinfection, cuticle care, trimming and filing, and basic color application under supervision. Learn hygiene and chemical safety procedures and retain process records.

Evidence to show: use a reviewable service record covering requirements confirmation, disinfection steps, finished results, and precautions to demonstrate the ability to follow hygiene procedures and document work accurately.

Next step: check the target employer's hiring requirements, state or local licensing and hygiene rules, and products and tools used. Validate practical skills and client communication in real services under supervision.

Moving toward greater responsibility: with experience, workers may manage appointments and client relationships, train newcomers, oversee hygiene and quality standards, or move into nail salon operations, education, or products.
Market signals and transition directions

Older facts retain employment of 210,100 in 2024 and the 2024—2034 projections; 24,800 should be interpreted as average annual openings. The latest BLS figures are 201,800 in 2025, 9% growth in 2025—2035, and 21,900 average annual openings. These are statistical projections, not a hiring sample or an individual's probability of being hired.

The main industry on that page for 2024 is Other Services (Except Public Administration). Employment and openings are statistical projections and must be interpreted separately from individual opportunities.

Transferable capabilities: hygiene and disinfection procedures, fine hand skills, client communication and requirements confirmation, safe product and chemical use, appointment and inventory record management, aesthetic judgment, and attention to detail.

Moving into barbering requires additional training in cutting hair, shaving, blade hygiene, and styling hair and beards, along with service authorization in the target jurisdiction. Fine hand skills and client communication experience do not establish competence in barbering.

risks.consequence: May cause cross-infection or hygiene problems.
risks.mitigation: After every client, clean and disinfect tools, workstations, and footbaths according to local procedures and product instructions. A UV storage box is not equivalent to tool disinfection.
risks.scenario: Tools or workstations do not meet cleaning and disinfection requirements.

risks.consequence: May cause discomfort or injury to clients or practitioners.
risks.mitigation: First check labels and SDS, exhaust ventilation, and product-appropriate protection. Dust protection is not solvent vapor protection; select protection according to the employer's assessment.
risks.scenario: Chemicals are not used according to labels, or ventilation is inadequate.

risks.consequence: May delay referral or worsen the problem.
risks.mitigation: Pause the relevant service when wounds, broken skin, or visible infection are present and refer according to procedures; do not diagnose or treat independently.
risks.scenario: Service continues despite unrecognized nail or skin abnormalities.

risks.consequence: May cause disputes and negative reviews.
risks.mitigation: Confirm needs, expected results, and prices before service.
risks.scenario: Needs, results, and prices have not been agreed with the client.

risks.consequence: May violate local hygiene and practice rules.
risks.mitigation: Verify licenses and permits under local requirements.
risks.scenario: Independently serving clients and collecting payments at a location without the appropriate license or permit.

risks.consequence: May affect hygiene and service quality.
risks.mitigation: Schedule appointments reasonably and allow time for disinfection and turnaround.
risks.scenario: Overlapping peak-hour appointments and insufficient workstation and tool turnaround.
risks.title: Loss of control over appointments and workstation arrangements

source_card.note: Check source scope, limitations, and statistical periods separately against the original evidence. Source usage notes: O*NET 39-5092.00 Manicurists and Pedicurists (Summary): provides occupational identity, the official description, interest code, Job Zone, skills, and knowledge for 39-5092.00. Wage and employment data on that page cover this occupation. O*NET 39-5092.00 Tasks: provides tasks such as cleaning and disinfection, cuticle treatment, trimming and filing, color and decoration, assessing hands, giving advice, maintaining inventory and records, scheduling appointments, and collecting payments. Task examples do not mean every position performs every task. O*NET 39-5092.00 Work Context: describes controlled indoor environments, exposure to contaminants, repetitive hand movements, responsibility for others' health and safety, and other contexts. US work context does not replace Chinese law or employer procedures. O*NET 39-5092.00 National Wages (BLS OEWS Display): 2025 BLS OEWS median wages, covering this occupation. This page does not display percentile wages. O*NET 39-5092.00 National Employment Trends: employment in 2024 and projections for growth and job openings in 2024—2034. Projections are not a hiring guarantee. Industries: 39-5092.00: the main industry on that page for 2024 is Other Services (Except Public Administration). Industry distribution signals employer settings, not projected growth or demand. O*NET 39-5092.00 Education and Occupational Preparation: Job Zone 1-2; a high-school diploma or GED is typically required, on-the-job training ranges from several days to one year, and most states require licensing. Education distribution does not establish mandatory requirements for every employer. Licenses & Certifications: 39-5092.00: O*NET provides state licensing and national certification lookup entry points. Certification and training do not equal authorization to practice or employer hiring requirements. Generative AI and Jobs (ILO Working Paper 140, 2025): assesses occupational exposure to generative AI at the task level. An exposure index is not an adoption rate, job outcome, or hiring probability. Average Annual Wages of Employees in Urban Units in 2025: provides average annual wages by industry category for urban non-private and private units, including residential services, repairs, and other services. Industry averages are not occupational medians and exclude individually owned businesses and freelancers. Enterprise Compensation Survey Information (2024): the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security's enterprise compensation survey information provides a pay lookup entry point by occupation / position. Covers urban enterprises, excluding government agencies and public institutions; this page did not obtain an exact occupational match. FermatMind Task Impact Scale for Manicurists and Pedicurists: organizes potentially assisted tasks and human control points for task-level AI and fit discussions. An editorial scale is not evidence of adoption rates, layoffs, regulations, or licensing.
